stages.title: Nuclear reactions
stages.hook: When a nucleus changes, what must stay the same before and after: the total number of protons, the total number of particles, or both?
explain: A nuclear equation shows how nuclei change. We write each nucleus with its mass number at the top and its atomic number at the bottom, for example uranium-238 as 238 over 92.

Two things are always conserved in a nuclear reaction: the total mass number (protons plus neutrons) and the total charge, which is shown by the atomic number. So the numbers on the left must add up to the same totals on the right.

In alpha decay, a nucleus emits an alpha particle (mass 4, atomic number 2). So the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2. In beta decay, a neutron turns into a proton and an electron is emitted: the mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes up by 1.
Gamma emission lets a nucleus drop to a lower energy state without changing its numbers.

example.q: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) emits an alpha particle. What nucleus is formed?
steps: Element 90 is thorium, so the new nucleus is thorium-234.

analogies.home: Money in a purse: when you swap coins for others, the total value stays the same.
analogies.sport: A team swaps players but the number of players on the pitch is unchanged.
analogies.city: A bus splits into two buses: total passengers stay the same.
analogies.tech: Like balancing a budget: both sides of the equation must match.

stages.mnemonic: Top numbers add up, bottom numbers add up: both sides must match.
terms: A way of writing a nuclear change with mass and atomic numbers.
A nucleus emits a helium nucleus.
A neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton, emitting an electron.
Having the same total before and after.

misc.wrong: In nuclear reactions the element always stays the same.
misc.right: Nuclear reactions can change one element into another because the number of protons changes. Chemical reactions cannot.

stages.limits: Beta decay also emits a tiny particle called an antineutrino, which this level leaves out.

They use much more heat than chemistry can
They use many more atoms at one time
They use water to move the electrons about

questions.q: Thorium-234 (atomic number 90) emits a beta particle. Name the new atomic number and explain how you know.
questions.model: The new atomic number is 91. In beta decay a neutron turns into a proton, so the atomic number rises by one while the mass number stays 234.
questions.why: Beta decay raises the atomic number by 1.

questions.q: A student writes: 238 → 236 + 4. Which equation check is relevant?
o: The mass numbers balance: 236 + 4 = 240, not 238
Nothing is wrong, since 236 + 4 equals 238
Only the charges are wrong, not the masses

panel.q: Why does the daughter nucleus after alpha decay usually have a different chemical behaviour?
o: It is a different element, with different electron arrangement
It gains extra neutrons, and that alone changes its chemical behaviour
It becomes a gas, whatever element it was before the decay
It stops being an atom once the alpha particle leaves
panel.why: A different proton number means a different element.

panel.q: Explain in your own words why mass number and atomic number must each add up on both sides of a nuclear equation.
panel.model: Protons and neutrons are not created or destroyed in these reactions, and electric charge is conserved, so the totals are equal before and after.
panel.why: Conservation laws hold.

panel.q: A source emits only gamma rays. After a long time, will its element change?

Yes, into lead after a long time
Yes, into hydrogen after a long time
It disappears completely after a long time
panel.why: Gamma emission does not change mass or atomic number.

teach.model: In a nuclear reaction, the total mass number and the total atomic number stay the same. In alpha decay the mass number drops by 4 and the atomic number by 2. In beta decay the mass number stays the same and the atomic number rises by 1. This can turn one element into another.

stages.title: Nuclear decay calculations
stages.hook: A medical isotope is delivered at noon on Monday. By Thursday, how much of it is left to use?
explain: The amount of a radioactive isotope that remains after time t is N = N₀ × (1/2)^(t ÷ T), where T is the half-life and N₀ is the starting amount. The exponent t ÷ T counts how many half-lives have passed.
If t ÷ T is a whole number, just halve that many times. For other values you can use a calculator, or reason between whole half-lives.
Activity A is the number of decays per second, in becquerels. Activity is proportional to the number of radioactive atoms left, so activity also halves every half-life.
We can also work backwards. If a sample has fallen to 1/16 of its original activity, then 4 half-lives have passed, because (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.

example.q: A sample of iodine-131 (half-life 8 days) has an activity of 640 kBq. What is the activity after 24 days?

analogies.home: Half the milk in a jug is drunk each day: 8 L, 4 L, 2 L, 1 L.
analogies.farm: A haystack halves every week for winter feed.
analogies.tech: A phone battery that loses half its remaining charge every hour.

stages.mnemonic: Count the half-lives, halve that many times.
terms: Time for the activity or number of atoms to halve.
The small raised number showing how many times to multiply.

misc.wrong: If half is gone after 1 day, all is gone after 2 days.
misc.right: After a second half-life only half of the remainder goes: a quarter is left.

stages.limits: For very small samples decay is too random to follow the smooth curve exactly.

questions.q: A hospital orders a tracer with a short half-life. Explain one advantage and one limit of this for planning.
questions.model: A short half-life means the radioactivity fades quickly so patients receive a lower total dose, but the tracer must be made or delivered close to the time of use because it cannot be stored for long.
questions.why: Both sides of the trade-off matter.

questions.q: A student says: 'two half-lives is a whole life, so it is all gone.' What is wrong?
o: Each half-life removes half of what is left, so one quarter remains
Nothing is wrong, because after two half-lives all the atoms have decayed away

Decay stops completely once two half-lives have passed

panel.q: Two samples start with equal activity. A has half-life 2 days and B has half-life 4 days. After 8 days, which has the higher activity?
o: B
A
Equal
Cannot tell
panel.why: A: 4 half-lives = 1/16. B: 2 half-lives = 1/4. So B is higher.

panel.q: Why does the activity of a sample fall in proportion to the number of atoms left?
panel.model: Each remaining atom has the same chance of decaying in a given time, so fewer atoms means fewer decays per second.
panel.why: Activity is proportional to the number of unstable atoms.

panel.q: A source reads 90 Bq on a day. A week later it reads 45 Bq. Which is a reasonable conclusion?
o: Its half-life is about one week
Its half-life is about 45 days
It is stable, and the count just fell by chance
Its half-life is about 90 days
panel.why: Activity halved in a week.

teach.model: First find how many half-lives have passed by dividing the time by the half-life. Then halve the starting amount that many times. For example, 640 units with a half-life of 8 days after 24 days: 3 half-lives, so 640 becomes 320, 160, 80.

stages.title: Radiation measurement
stages.hook: We cannot see, hear or feel most radiation. How can anyone know it is there?
explain: We detect radiation with instruments. A Geiger–Müller counter clicks each time radiation ionises the gas in its tube. A scintillation detector gives a flash of light. A film badge or electronic dosimeter records the dose a worker has received.

We use different units. Activity (how many decays per second) is measured in becquerels (Bq). Absorbed dose (energy deposited per kilogram) is measured in grays (Gy). Equivalent or effective dose (which takes into account how harmful the kind of radiation is) is measured in sieverts (Sv). Everyday doses are small, so we use millisieverts (mSv) and microsieverts (µSv).
A detector always counts some background radiation from rocks, air and space. To measure a sample we count with the sample, count without it, and subtract the background.
Counts are random, so we count for a longer time to improve accuracy.

example.q: A counter gives 540 counts in 1 minute with a sample and 60 counts in 1 minute with no sample. What is the count rate due to the sample?

analogies.sport: A scoreboard counts each goal; the Geiger counter counts each click.
analogies.home: A water meter counts litres, a radiation meter counts decays.
analogies.city: A traffic counter at a road records every car; subtract the buses to count the cars.
analogies.nature: A rain gauge collects drops over time.

stages.mnemonic: Bq counts the decays, Gy counts the energy, Sv counts the effect on the body.
terms: Dose adjusted for the biological effect.
An instrument that clicks when radiation enters.
The count with no sample present.

misc.wrong: Becquerels and sieverts measure the same thing.
misc.right: Becquerels measure how active a source is. Sieverts measure the effect of radiation on a person.

stages.limits: A counter reading depends on the kind and energy of radiation and on its distance from the source.

questions.q: A source reads high when close but low when 2 metres away. What is the best conclusion?
o: Distance reduces the reading
The source changed element
The detector is shielded by the floor only
Radiation does not spread

Add the background rate to the rate with the sample
Multiply the two measured rates together
Use only the background rate by itself

panel.q: Two sources have the same activity in becquerels, one emits alpha and one gamma. Why might their effects on a person differ?
o: Different radiation types deposit energy differently and travel differently
They cannot differ at all, because the activity in becquerels is the same for both
Becquerels measure the weight of the source, not its decays
Alpha is a kind of sound, not a kind of radiation
panel.why: Activity is not the same as dose.

panel.q: Why do we use the sievert and not just the number of decays when judging risk to people?
panel.model: The number of decays does not tell us how much energy a person absorbs or how damaging that radiation type is. The sievert accounts for energy absorbed and the biological effect.
panel.why: Risk depends on dose, not on activity alone.

panel.q: A measurement is 20% above the usual background in one reading. Why should you not panic at once?
o: Counts naturally vary, so repeat and average
Background never varies from one reading to the next
A rise of 20% is always a deadly level
Detectors always lie, so ignore the result
panel.why: Random variation is normal.

teach.model: A Geiger counter clicks when radiation passes through it. Becquerels count decays per second, and sieverts measure the effect on a person. Because there is always background radiation, you measure it first and subtract it from your reading.

stages.title: Neutron interactions
stages.hook: Neutrons have no charge, so they can slip right up to a nucleus. What happens when they arrive?
explain: A neutron has no charge, so it is not pushed away by the positive nucleus. This makes neutrons very good at causing nuclear reactions. A neutron can scatter (bounce off), be absorbed (captured), or cause fission.

Neutrons from fission are fast. But fission in uranium-235 happens much more easily with slow neutrons. A moderator is a material of light atoms, such as water or graphite, that slows neutrons down by collisions, like a ball losing speed bouncing off other balls.

Some materials absorb neutrons strongly, for example boron and cadmium. Control rods are made of such materials. Pushing them in absorbs more neutrons and reduces the number of fissions. Pulling them out allows more.
Neutrons themselves are difficult to stop with thin metals. Hydrogen-rich materials such as water, concrete and plastic are good at slowing them, and then boron can absorb them.

example.q: Why does a moderator use light atoms and not heavy ones?
steps: A neutron loses most energy when it hits something of similar mass.
Light atoms (like hydrogen) have a mass close to a neutron's.
Heavy atoms just bounce the neutron off with little loss.
example.a: Because collisions with light atoms slow neutrons most

analogies.sport: A billiard ball hitting another ball of the same size slows down a lot. Hitting a heavy bowling ball it just bounces back at nearly the same speed.
analogies.home: A sponge soaks up water like boron soaks up neutrons.
analogies.city: A traffic jam slows fast cars down, like a moderator.
analogies.sea: A swimmer slowed by a thick crowd.

stages.mnemonic: Moderator Makes neutrons slower; control rods Cut the count.
terms: A rod that absorbs neutrons to control fission.
A neutron bouncing off a nucleus.

misc.wrong: Control rods are what make the reactor hot.
misc.right: Control rods absorb neutrons and so reduce fission. The heat comes from fission in the fuel.

stages.limits: Different reactors use different moderators, and some use fast neutrons without any moderator.

questions.q: Explain why fast neutrons are slowed down in many reactors before they meet more fuel.
questions.model: Slow neutrons are much more likely to cause fission in uranium-235, so a moderator slows the fast neutrons from fission through collisions with light atoms.
questions.why: The chance of fission is higher for slow neutrons.

questions.q: A neutron is captured by a nucleus without causing fission. What has happened?

The neutron changed into an electron and escaped from the nucleus

questions.q: Why is a water tank a good shield for neutrons?

Water is clear, so neutrons can see through it

questions.why: Hydrogen-rich materials slow neutrons effectively.

panel.q: If a moderator were removed from a reactor that depends on slow neutrons, what would you expect?
o: The fission rate would fall
The fission rate would rise sharply
Nothing would change
More heat would be made

panel.q: A boron-containing material is placed behind water in a shield. Explain why both parts help.
panel.model: Water slows the fast neutrons, and boron then absorbs the slowed neutrons, so together they remove them effectively.
panel.why: Slowing then absorbing is a common shielding pattern.

panel.q: Neutrons are not charged, so a magnet cannot steer them. What does this imply for neutron control?

Neutrons cannot be controlled by any method

teach.topic: How neutrons are slowed and absorbed
teach.model: Neutrons have no charge, so they can reach nuclei easily. A moderator such as water slows them by collisions, because light atoms take away more of their energy. Control rods made of boron or cadmium absorb neutrons to control fission.

stages.title: Reactor components
stages.hook: If you had to build a safe machine to boil water with atoms, what parts would it need?
explain: A reactor core holds the fuel: small ceramic pellets of uranium oxide stacked inside long metal tubes called fuel rods. Many rods make a fuel assembly.
The moderator slows neutrons. The control rods absorb neutrons. The coolant, often water, flows past the fuel and carries heat away. All of this sits inside a thick steel reactor pressure vessel.
Around the vessel is a strong containment building, usually made of reinforced concrete and steel. It is a last barrier to protect people and the environment.

In a pressurised water reactor, the hot water in the core is kept under high pressure so it does not boil. It passes through a steam generator, where it heats a separate loop of water into steam that spins the turbine.

example.q: A fuel assembly has 200 fuel rods. A core holds 150 assemblies. How many fuel rods are in the core?

analogies.home: A boiler has a flame (fuel), a thermostat (control) and a pipe system (coolant).
analogies.farm: A grain store has bins (fuel rods), locks (control) and walls (containment).
analogies.sea: A ship has an engine, a rudder to steer and a strong hull.
analogies.city: A city's power plant sits inside layers: fence, wall, building.

Where reactor heat makes steam in a separate loop.

misc.wrong: The fuel is a liquid that is poured in.
misc.right: Most power reactor fuel is solid ceramic pellets sealed in metal tubes.

stages.limits: This describes common water-cooled reactors. Other designs use gas, liquid metal or molten salt as coolant.

panel.q: Which sequence lists physical barriers from the fuel outward?

panel.q: Why is it useful that a reactor has several different kinds of barrier rather than just one very thick one?
panel.model: Different barriers stop different problems and if one fails the next still protects, which is the idea of defence in depth.
panel.why: Multiple independent layers are more robust.

panel.q: A designer chooses water as both coolant and moderator. What is one consequence?

teach.model: A reactor core holds fuel rods. A moderator slows neutrons and control rods absorb them. Coolant carries heat away to make steam. The core is inside a steel vessel and a strong containment building, which are layers of protection.

stages.title: Nuclear energy conversion
stages.hook: Only about a third of the heat from a typical power station becomes electricity. Where does the rest go?
explain: In a nuclear power station, energy changes form in a chain: nuclear energy in the fuel becomes heat, heat makes steam, steam has movement energy that spins the turbine, and the generator turns that movement into electrical energy.

Efficiency is useful energy out divided by total energy in. Thermal power stations, including nuclear, are about 30 to 40 percent efficient. The rest of the heat is released in a condenser to cooling water or the air.
Power is energy per second, measured in watts (W). A megawatt (MW) is a million watts. We write MWt for thermal power from the reactor and MWe for electrical power.
Nuclear fuel is very energy-dense. A pellet of uranium fuel about the size of a fingertip can release about as much energy as a tonne of coal.

example.q: A reactor makes 3000 MW of heat. The station is 33% efficient. How many MW of electricity does it produce?

analogies.sport: A cyclist turns only part of the food energy into motion; the rest becomes heat.
analogies.home: A car engine wastes much of the fuel's energy as heat.
analogies.city: A water mill turns flowing water into power with some loss to friction.
analogies.farm: A cow turns grass energy into milk, but much is lost as body heat.

stages.mnemonic: Nuclear to heat to steam to spin to electricity: N-H-S-S-E.

Energy transferred per second, in watts.
Where used steam is cooled back to water.

misc.right: Energy is conserved. The rest is transferred as waste heat to the surroundings.

stages.limits: Real efficiencies depend on the design and the temperature of the cooling water.

Shielding; it blocks the radiation from the core
Decay; it creates heat from the waste itself
questions.why: Using the waste heat improves overall energy use.

panel.q: A claim says a power station with 33% efficiency 'wastes' two thirds. What is a fairer statement?
o: Two thirds becomes low-grade heat that is hard to turn into electricity
It is destroyed inside the plant, so none of it can be reused anywhere
It all becomes radioactive material that must be stored for centuries
It is turned directly back into new fuel for the reactor core
panel.why: The energy is conserved but not easily useful.

panel.q: Why does a station need a source of cooling water such as a river, sea or cooling tower?
panel.model: The steam leaving the turbine must be cooled and condensed back into water so it can be reused, and the waste heat has to go somewhere such as a river, sea or the air.
panel.why: Heat rejection completes the cycle.

panel.q: A station's cooling water is returned warmer to a river. What is a fair concern?
o: It can affect river life, so limits and monitoring are used
Nothing can ever happen to the river at all
Heat alone is enough to make the river radioactive
The river will dry up and disappear completely
panel.why: Thermal discharge is regulated for ecological reasons.

teach.model: Fission heats water into steam. The steam spins a turbine and the turbine drives a generator that makes electricity. About a third of the heat becomes electricity. The rest leaves as waste heat through a condenser to cooling water or air.

stages.title: Reactor cooling fundamentals
stages.hook: A reactor is switched off, but the core keeps making heat for days. Why, and how is it kept cool?
explain: The coolant carries heat from the fuel. The heat energy needed to warm a mass m of water by a temperature change ΔT is Q = m × c × ΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. For water, c is about 4200 J per kg per °C.
Water is a good coolant because it has a high specific heat capacity, so it absorbs a lot of heat for a small rise in temperature. It is also cheap and also acts as a moderator in many reactors.

Even after a reactor shuts down, the radioactive fission products in the fuel keep decaying and giving off heat. This is called decay heat. It starts at a few percent of full power and then falls over hours and days, but it must still be removed.
Safety systems therefore include pumps, backup power supplies and in some designs passive systems that use gravity and natural circulation to keep cooling the core without needing power.

example.q: How much heat is needed to warm 50 kg of water by 20 °C? (c = 4200 J/kg°C)

analogies.home: A radiator carries heat away from a car engine, just as coolant carries heat from the core.
analogies.nature: Sea water warms slowly and cools slowly because water holds a lot of heat.
analogies.sport: A runner needs a drink after the race: the body keeps producing heat for a while after stopping.
analogies.farm: A pond used to cool animal sheds.

stages.mnemonic: Q = m c ΔT: mass, material, temperature change.
terms: Energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.
Heat from radioactive decay that continues after shutdown.
Fluid moving because hot fluid rises and cold sinks.
Safety that works without pumps or operator action.

misc.wrong: When the chain reaction stops, the core stops making heat.
misc.right: Decay of fission products still makes heat after shutdown, so cooling must continue.

stages.limits: The decay-heat percentage depends on how long the reactor ran. The same ideas apply to spent fuel stored in pools.

trip.prompt: Find the graph of decay heat after shutdown and see how quickly it falls.

questions.q: How many joules are needed to warm 10 kg of water by 30 °C? (c = 4200 J/kg°C)
A coolant absorbs 840 000 J and warms by 20 °C. Its mass is 10 kg. What is its specific heat capacity in J/kg°C?
Why is water a good coolant?
o: It has a high specific heat capacity
It is dark, so it absorbs heat well
It has no mass, so it flows easily
It is magnetic, so it sticks to the fuel
questions.why: It can absorb a lot of heat per kilogram.

questions.q: What is decay heat?
o: Heat from radioactive fission products after shutdown
Heat that arrives from the Sun through the roof
Heat from friction in the pumps only
Heat from burning coal in a nearby plant
questions.why: Radioactive decay continues after fission stops.

questions.q: Why must cooling continue after a reactor is shut down?
o: The fuel still produces decay heat
The fuel is already cold after shutdown
The control rods warm up when they are inserted
The water would otherwise be wasted
questions.why: Without cooling, the fuel could overheat and be damaged.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.why: Cooling concepts link together.

questions.q: Explain why backup power matters for reactor cooling.
questions.model: Pumps need electricity to circulate coolant, and decay heat continues after shutdown, so if the grid power is lost backup supplies are needed to keep the core cooled.
questions.why: Loss of cooling was the central problem in the Fukushima accident in 2011.

questions.q: A passive cooling system uses a tank of water high above the core. What makes it flow down?
o: Gravity
A pump
A magnet
A fan
questions.why: Gravity-driven flow needs no power.

questions.q: Order the cooling story after shutdown.
questions.why: Fission stops quickly, but decay heat falls slowly as short-lived products decay.

questions.q: Two coolants are compared. A has a higher specific heat capacity than B. For the same flow and heat, which warms up less?
o: A
B
Same
Neither warms
questions.why: More energy per degree means a smaller rise in temperature.

panel.q: Why is decay heat a design driver even for a reactor that is off?
o: Cooling must be reliable at all times
It makes chain reactions start by themselves
It makes electricity even when the reactor is off
It changes the colour of the fuel pellets
panel.why: Reliable cooling is essential to protect the fuel.

panel.q: Give one advantage and one limit of passive safety systems.
panel.model: Passive systems work without power or operators, relying on gravity or natural circulation. But their driving forces are small, so they may remove less heat and must be carefully designed.
panel.why: Every design choice has trade-offs.

panel.q: A river used for cooling is very low in a hot dry summer. What is a fair operational response?
o: Reduce power to keep within safe and environmental limits
Ignore the limits and keep running at full power to meet demand
Add more fuel to the core to make up for the low river
Remove the control rods to raise the power and use less water
panel.why: Operators follow limits on cooling and discharge.

teach.model: Coolant, usually water, carries heat away from the fuel. Water is good because it holds a lot of heat per kilogram. Even after shutdown, radioactive decay keeps making heat, so cooling must continue, with backup power or passive systems.

points.ask: What happens when it is switched off?

stages.title: Radiation shielding concepts
stages.hook: If you walk away from a campfire, you feel less heat. How fast does it fade, and what if you put up a wall?
explain: From a small source, radiation spreads out in all directions. The intensity falls with the square of the distance: double the distance and the intensity is one quarter. This is the inverse square law.

Shielding reduces radiation by placing absorbing material between source and person. Each material has a half-value layer: the thickness that cuts the intensity to half. Two half-value layers cut it to one quarter, and three to one eighth.

Different radiations need different shields. Paper stops alpha. A few millimetres of aluminium stops most beta. Dense materials such as lead or thick concrete are used for gamma rays. Hydrogen-rich materials such as water slow neutrons, and boron then absorbs them.
Good protection combines time, distance and shielding, and is designed to keep doses as low as reasonably achievable, the ALARA principle.

example.q: The dose rate is 80 µSv/h at 1 m from a small gamma source. What is it at 4 m?

analogies.home: A torch lights a small spot when close to a wall, but spreads thin when far away.
analogies.sport: The noise from a stadium fades as you walk away.
analogies.city: A wall between you and a loud road cuts the noise.

stages.mnemonic: Double the distance, quarter the dose. Each half-layer halves it.
terms: Intensity falls with the square of the distance.
Keep doses as low as reasonably achievable.

misc.right: Shielding reduces radiation by a factor; more thickness reduces it more, but it never reaches exactly zero.

stages.limits: The inverse square law applies to a small source in open space. Real shielding designs depend on energy and geometry.

trip.prompt: Find the three protective factors and one example of each.

questions.q: A small source gives 120 µSv/h at 1 m. What is the dose rate at 2 m (µSv/h)?
questions.why: Distance doubles so intensity is divided by 4: 120 ÷ 4 = 30.

questions.q: A source gives 90 µSv/h at 1 m. What is the dose rate at 3 m (µSv/h)?
questions.why: Distance 3 times larger → divide by 9: 90 ÷ 9 = 10.

questions.q: Radiation has intensity 64 units. A shield is 3 half-value layers thick. What intensity gets through?
The half-value layer of a lead shield is 1 cm for a gamma source. The intensity is 400 units. What is the intensity behind 4 cm of lead?
questions.why: 4 half-value layers: 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 → 25.

questions.q: If you double your distance from a small source, the intensity becomes...
o: One quarter
One half of the intensity
The same intensity as before
Double the intensity
questions.why: Inverse square law.

questions.q: Which material is best suited to shielding gamma rays?
o: Thick lead or concrete
A single sheet of paper
A thin plastic bag
A piece of cotton cloth
questions.why: Dense, thick material absorbs penetrating gamma rays.

questions.q: What does ALARA stand for in spirit?
o: Keep exposure as low as reasonably achievable
Maximum safe exposure should always be allowed
Avoid all radiation at any cost, whatever the benefit
Allow as much radiation at work as the law lets
questions.why: It balances protection and practicality.

questions.q: A technician must work near a gamma source for 10 minutes. Describe two ways to reduce the dose, using time, distance or shielding.
questions.model: She can work more quickly to reduce time, stay farther from the source or use tongs for distance, and place a lead or concrete shield between herself and the source.
questions.why: Time, distance and shielding all lower dose.

questions.q: Why is lead a common shield for gamma rays?
o: It is dense and absorbs gamma well
It is light
It is cheap and slows neutrons by hydrogen
It reflects all radiation
questions.why: Dense materials with many electrons absorb gamma effectively.

questions.q: A worker says: 'I stood at the corner of the room, so I got no dose.' What is the best reply?
o: Distance reduces dose but does not make it zero
She is right, because corners are always safe
Corners remove radiation completely from the room
Dose is the same everywhere in the room
questions.why: Dose falls with distance, but shielding and monitoring are still needed.

panel.q: A 2 cm concrete wall halves the radiation. Roughly how thick should it be to reduce the radiation to one eighth?
o: 6 cm
4 cm
8 cm
3 cm
panel.why: One eighth needs three half-value layers: 3 × 2 cm = 6 cm.

panel.q: Why is water a useful shield around spent fuel stored in a pool?
panel.model: Water absorbs and slows radiation, including neutrons, while also cooling the fuel. Workers can see and handle fuel under water with remote tools.
panel.why: A pool shields and cools at the same time.

panel.q: Why is ALARA a better rule than a fixed idea of 'perfectly safe'?
o: Any added dose carries a small risk, so it is minimised sensibly
Radiation is harmless in all amounts, so no limit is ever needed
Costs do not matter in nuclear work, so any exposure is acceptable
Doses never add up over a working year, so only single doses count
panel.why: ALARA reflects that doses should be kept low, balancing risk and practical benefit.

teach.model: Radiation gets weaker as you move away: double the distance and it is a quarter. A shield made of a suitable material cuts it by half for every half-value layer. Use time, distance and shielding together to keep dose as low as reasonably achievable.

points.ask: What happens as I move away?
How thick should a shield be?

stages.title: Radioactive waste management
stages.hook: Almost every energy source leaves something behind. What should we do with the waste from nuclear power?
explain: Radioactive waste is sorted by how radioactive it is and how long it stays so. Low-level waste, such as gloves, tools and clothing, is short-lived and mostly handled in simple engineered disposal sites. Intermediate-level waste needs shielding. High-level waste, mainly used fuel and its separated products, is hot and strongly radioactive.
Used fuel is first stored for years in cooling pools of water, which cool and shield it. After that it can be moved into dry storage in thick concrete and steel casks.

For long-term disposal, many countries plan deep geological repositories, in stable rock hundreds of metres underground, with several barriers: the waste form, metal canisters, clay or other buffer and the rock itself. Finland has been building one at Onkalo.

The total volume of high-level waste from nuclear power is small compared with the waste from many other industries, but it needs to be isolated for a very long time. Societies disagree about how and where to do this, and public trust and consent matter.

example.q: A waste has activity 800 kBq and its main isotope has a half-life of 30 years. About what will the activity be after 90 years?

analogies.home: A household sorts rubbish into recycling, compost and hazardous items like batteries.
analogies.city: A city has landfill for ordinary rubbish and special sites for dangerous waste.
analogies.farm: Compost heaps are kept apart from the animals.
analogies.sea: Ship fuel waste is stored in sealed tanks.

stages.mnemonic: Sort it, cool it, shield it, bury it deep.
terms: Slightly radioactive items such as gloves and tools.
Strongly radioactive, heat-producing waste such as used fuel.
A secure facility for long-term disposal.
Several layers that each hold waste in.

misc.wrong: All nuclear waste stays dangerous for ever.
misc.right: Radioactivity falls with time. Most waste decays quickly; the longest-lived part needs isolation for a very long time.

stages.limits: Experts and communities disagree on the best long-term solutions, such as repositories, reprocessing or interim storage.

trip.prompt: Find a picture of a repository design. Count the barriers between the waste and the surface.

questions.q: Which waste is the least radioactive?
o: Low-level waste such as gloves
Used fuel
High-level waste
Reactor core metal in operation
questions.why: Low-level waste has low activity.

questions.q: Why is used fuel first stored in water pools?
o: Water cools and shields it
Water makes it radioactive
Water speeds decay
Water removes all radioactivity
questions.why: Pools remove decay heat and block radiation.

questions.q: A waste sample has an activity of 1600 kBq. Its half-life is 10 years. What is its activity after 40 years (kBq)?
A waste isotope has a half-life of 5 years. How many years until its activity is 1/8 of the start?
questions.why: 1/8 is 3 half-lives, 3 × 5 = 15 years.

questions.q: What is a deep geological repository?
o: A facility in stable rock deep underground for long-term isolation
A cooling pool on the surface where used fuel is kept for a few years
A rocket that carries the waste away from the Earth into space
A shipping port where waste is loaded onto boats and moved about
questions.why: It uses the rock as one of several barriers.

questions.q: Order the stages in managing used fuel.
questions.why: The stages follow decreasing heat and time.

questions.q: Match the waste to a typical handling.
questions.why: More radioactive and longer-lived waste needs stronger isolation.

questions.q: Why is it useful to have several barriers in a repository rather than relying on rock alone?
questions.model: Several barriers (waste form, canister, buffer, rock) each slow or stop the release of radioactive material, so if one fails the others still protect people and the environment.
questions.why: This applies defence in depth to waste.

questions.q: A community near a proposed repository is worried. What is a fair response?
o: Share evidence openly and involve them in decisions
Ignore the concerns, since the plan is fixed
Hide the data until the work has been done
Decide for them without any discussion at all
questions.why: Trust and consent are central to waste siting.

questions.q: Which statement compares waste fairly?
o: Nuclear waste is small in volume but needs long isolation, while other energy sources also produce waste or emissions
Only nuclear power produces any waste, so it should be avoided altogether
Nuclear waste is harmless, so it needs no isolation at all
Other energy sources produce no waste or emissions of any kind
questions.why: All energy systems have waste or environmental impacts.

panel.q: Why does the half-life of a waste isotope influence how it is managed?
o: Short half-life waste decays away sooner, while long half-life waste needs very long isolation
It does not matter how long a waste isotope lasts, as all waste is handled the same
Only the colour of the waste matters when choosing how to store it
A long half-life means it gives off no radiation at all, so it needs no care
panel.why: Time needed for decay sets storage planning.

panel.q: Present one argument in favour of and one against a deep repository for high-level waste.
panel.model: For: it isolates waste in stable rock with multiple barriers, so future generations need not actively guard it. Against: it must work for a very long time and some people worry about uncertainty, trust, cost and the ability to retrieve the waste.
panel.why: A fair answer states both views.

panel.q: Why is it considered ethical to plan waste disposal before building new power stations?
o: Those who benefit should not leave the burden to future generations
Waste is not an issue for any power station, so planning it is a waste of time
Plans never change, so they are best made early and not checked again
Future generations will be happy to pay for it, whatever it costs
panel.why: Responsibility across generations is an ethical principle.

teach.model: Radioactive waste is sorted by how strong and how long-lasting it is. Used fuel is cooled in water pools, then stored in dry casks. For the longest-lived waste, many countries plan deep repositories with several barriers. People still debate how best to do it, so openness and trust matter.

points.ask: What happens first to used fuel?
